subject: religious-studies
title: Augustine and the Fall
welcome_lead: Enter Augustine's North African study, where Eden's fall casts long shadows on the problem of evil.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on the Augustinian theodicy.
final_note: Whether Augustine convinces or not, his vision of evil as parasitic on good still shapes Christian theology.

concepts.def: Augustine's view that evil is not a substance but a privation of good, a falling-away from being.
The claim that moral evil is the price of genuine free creatures who can love.
The doctrine that humanity inherits guilt and corrupted nature from Adam, transmitted by generation.
Augustine's notion that all humanity was 'in Adam' at the Fall and therefore shares his guilt.
'Happy fault'; the Easter Vigil's celebration of the Fall as occasioning the greater good of Christ's redemption.
A modern logical defence (1974) showing it is possible that even an omnipotent God could not create free creatures who never sin.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Augustine (354-430), in Confessions, City of God, and On Free Choice of the Will, holds that God created a perfect world. Evil is not a thing but a deficiency, a turning of the will away from God to lesser goods.

The angelic fall and then the human fall in Eden introduced sin into creation. Natural evil is, on Augustine's view, a consequence of moral evil and cosmic disorder.

Schleiermacher objected that a perfect world cannot go wrong without already containing imperfection. If Adam was perfect, he could not have sinned; if he sinned, he was not perfect.

Modern critics question whether all of humanity can be justly held responsible for Adam's sin and whether the doctrine sits well with evolution and an old earth.

Alvin Plantinga's God, Freedom, and Evil (1974) revives the free will defence in modal logic. He argues that it is logically possible that every creaturely essence suffers from 'transworld depravity' so that any world of free creatures will contain some evil.

Plantinga's argument is widely regarded as a successful response to Mackie's logical problem.

mcqs.q: Augustine views evil as which of the following?
options: A privation of good
A second principle
An illusion
A divine action

mcqs.q: Whose 1974 book God, Freedom, and Evil defends the free will defence?
options: Alvin Plantinga
John Hick
Richard Swinburne
Bertrand Russell

mcqs.q: What distinction matters for the free will defence to the problem of evil?
options: Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.
It is the question of whether the devil really exists.
The free will defence solves all forms of evil at once.

Between moral evil (caused by free human choices) and natural evil (earthquakes, disease) — the free will defence directly addresses moral evil but struggles with natural evil, which isn't a product of free choice.

mcqs.q: What is the problem of evil?
options: It is the question of whether the devil really exists.
It is the question of whether evil people will go to hell.
If God is all-loving, all-knowing and all-powerful, why does evil and suffering exist? Logically, all four cannot be true together without explanation.
Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.
